en: Majjhima Nikāya 8: The Discourse on Effacement.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Mahācunda emerged from seclusion and approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable...
Mahācunda said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, as for these various views that arise in the world—
whether connected with a doctrine of self or connected with a doctrine about the world— "
“Venerable sir, is it by attending to the very beginning that a bhikkhu achieves the abandoning of these views and the relinquishing of these views?
“Cunda, as for these various kinds of views that arise in the world—
whether connected with theories of self or connected with theories of the world— ”
Wherever these views arise, wherever they persist, and wherever they are practiced—one who sees this as it truly is with right wisdom, thinking:
"This is not mine; this I am not; this is not my self"—for such a person there comes the abandoning of these views, and for such a person there comes the relinquishing of these views.
"It is possible, Cunda, that here some bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures,
secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.
It might occur to him thus:"
‘I dwell in effacement.
But these, Cunda, are not called effacement in the Noble One’s discipline;
rather, in the Noble One’s discipline, these are called pleasant abidings in this very life.
But it is possible, Cunda, that here some bhikkhu, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought,
enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
It might occur to him:
"I dwell in effacement.
But these, Cunda, are not called effacement in the discipline of the Noble One.
"These are called 'abidings in happiness in this very life' in the discipline of the Noble One.

Furthermore, Cunda, it is possible that here a certain bhikkhu, with the fading away of rapture, may abide in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experience happiness with the body—of which the Noble Ones declare: [‘He who has equanimity and is mindful dwells happily’]."
‘Equanimous, mindful, and dwelling in happiness,’ he would enter and dwell in the third jhāna.
It would occur to him:
‘I am dwelling in effacement.’
But these, Cunda, are not called "effacement" in the discipline of the Noble One.
These are called "abidings in happiness in this very life" in the discipline of the Noble One.
It is possible, Cunda, that here some bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain...

And with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he might enter and dwell in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
It would occur to him thus:
‘I dwell in effacement.
But these, Cunda, are not called effacement in the Noble One’s discipline;
in the Noble One’s discipline, these are called pleasant dwellings in this very life.
It is possible, Cunda, that here some bhikkhu, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form,
with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking, ‘Space is infinite,’ might enter and dwell in the base of infinite space.
It might occur to him:
"I dwell in effacement.
But these, Cunda, are not called effacement in the discipline of the Noble One.
"These abodes are called peaceful in the discipline of the Noble One.

Furthermore, Cunda, it is possible that here a certain bhikkhu, having completely transcended the base of infinite space, might enter and dwell in the base of infinite consciousness, thinking: 'Consciousness is infinite.
It might occur to him thus:"
‘I dwell in effacement.
But these, Cunda, are not called effacement in the Noble One’s discipline;
rather, these are called peaceful abidings in the Noble One’s discipline.
Furthermore, Cunda, it is possible that here some bhikkhu, having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, thinking ‘there is nothing,’ enters and dwells in the base of nothingness.
It might occur to him:
‘I dwell in effacement.’
But these, Cunda, are not called "effacement" in the Noble One’s discipline;
rather, these are called "peaceful abidings" in the Noble One’s discipline.
It is possible, Cunda, that here some bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of nothingness, enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
It might occur to him:
"I dwell in effacement.
But these, Cunda, are not called effacement in the discipline of the Noble One.
"These abodes are called 'peaceful' in the discipline of the Noble One.
Furthermore, Cunda, here you must practice effacement."
‘Others will be harmful; we shall be harmless here’—thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will take life; we shall abstain from taking life here’—thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will take what is not given; we shall abstain from taking what is not given here’—thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will be unchaste; we shall be chaste here,’ thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will be speakers of falsehood; we shall abstain from falsehood here,’ thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will be speakers of divisive speech; we shall abstain from divisive speech here,’ thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will be harsh in speech; we, however, shall abstain from harsh speech here’—thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will be idle chatterers; we, however, shall abstain from idle chatter here’—thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will be covetous; we, however, shall be uncovetous here’—thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will have minds of ill will; we shall here have minds free from ill will’—thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will hold wrong view; we shall here hold right view’—thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will have wrong intention; we shall here have right intention’—thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will be of wrong speech; we shall be of right speech here’—effacement should be practiced.
‘Others will be of wrong action; we shall be of right action here’—effacement should be practiced.
‘Others will be of wrong livelihood; we shall be of right livelihood here’—effacement should be practiced.
‘Others will have wrong effort; we shall have right effort here,’ thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will have wrong mindfulness; we shall have right mindfulness here,’ thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will have wrong concentration; we shall have right concentration here,’ thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will have wrong knowledge; we shall here have right knowledge’—effacement should be practiced.
‘Others will have wrong liberation; we shall here have right liberation’—effacement should be practiced.
‘Others will be obsessed by sloth and torpor; we shall here be free from sloth and torpor’—effacement should be practiced.
‘Others will be restless; we shall be undisturbed here’—thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will be full of doubt; we shall be beyond doubt here’—thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will be angry; we shall be without anger here’—thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will be resentful; we shall be without resentment here,’ thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will be contemptuous; we shall be without contempt here,’ thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will be insolent; we shall be without insolence here,’ thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will be envious; we shall be free from envy here,’ thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will be miserly; we shall be free from miserliness here,’ thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will be deceitful; we shall be free from deceit here,’ thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will be deceitful; we shall be free from deceit here’—thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will be stubborn; we shall be free from stubbornness here’—thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will be conceited; we shall be free from conceit here’—thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will be difficult to speak with; we shall be easy to speak with here,’ thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will have evil friends; we shall have virtuous friends here,’ thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will be negligent; we shall be diligent here,’ thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will be faithless; we shall be faithful here,’ thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will be shameless; we shall be possessed of shame here,’ thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will be without moral dread; we shall be morally afraid here,’ thus should effacement be practiced.
‘Others will be of little learning; we shall be very learned here’—effacement should be practiced.
‘Others will be lazy; we shall be energetic here’—effacement should be practiced.
‘Others will be muddle-minded; we shall be established in mindfulness here’—effacement should be practiced.
‘Others will be deficient in wisdom; we shall here be endowed with wisdom’—thus should effacement be practiced.

‘Others will be attached to their own views, obstinate in grasping them, and difficult to release from them; we shall here not be attached to our own views, not obstinate in grasping them, and easy to release from them’—thus should effacement be practiced.
2. The Exposition on the Arising of the Mind (Cittuppāda-paryāya)
“Cunda, I say that even the mere arising of a thought is of great benefit regarding wholesome states, let alone acting in accordance with them through body and speech.
Therefore, Cunda, one should arouse the thought: ‘Others will be harmful; we shall be harmless here.
One should arouse the thought: ‘Others will take life; we shall abstain from taking life here. … [and so on].”

‘Others will be those who cling to their own views, who grasp tenaciously, and who are difficult to dislodge from them; we, however, shall be those here who do not cling to our own views, who do not grasp tenaciously, and who are easy to dislodge,’ such a thought should be aroused.
3. The Method of the Circuitous Path:
Just as, Cunda, there might be an uneven path, and another even path for its circuitous detour;
Or again, Cunda, just as there might be a difficult crossing where there is another, easy crossing for the purpose of traversing it;
even so, Cunda, for a person who is harmful, non-harming is the way to traverse it;
for a person who takes life, abstaining from taking life is the way to traverse it; for a person who takes what is not given...
Abstinence from taking what is not given is a means of protection; for a person who is unchaste, abstinence from unchastity is a means of protection;
for a person who speaks falsehood, abstinence from false speech is a means of protection;
for a person who speaks divisively, abstinence from divisive speech is a means of protection.
For a person who speaks harshly, abstaining from harsh speech is the way of retreat;
for a person who indulges in idle chatter, abstaining from idle chatter is the way of retreat;
for a person who is covetous, non-covetousness is the way of retreat; for a person with a mind of ill will, non-ill will is the way of retreat.
For a person of wrong view, right view arises as a means of escape;
for a person of wrong intention, right intention arises as a means of escape;
for a person of wrong speech, right speech arises as a means of escape; for a person of wrong action, right action arises [as a means of escape].
Right livelihood serves as the remedy for a person of wrong livelihood;
right effort serves as the remedy for a person of wrong effort; right mindfulness serves as the remedy for a person of wrong mindfulness;
and right concentration serves as the remedy for a person of wrong concentration.
For a person of wrong knowledge, right knowledge becomes the means of overcoming; for a person of wrong liberation, right liberation becomes the means of overcoming.
For a person overwhelmed by sloth and torpor, freedom from sloth and torpor becomes the means of overcoming.
For a person who is restless, non-restlessness is the means of overcoming;
for a person who is skeptical, the crossing beyond doubt is the means of overcoming; for a person who is angry, non-anger is the means of overcoming;
for a person who is resentful, non-resentment is the means of overcoming; for a person who is contemptuous...
For a person who is spiteful, lack of spite is the means of escape; for a person who is malicious, lack of malice is the means of escape;
for a person who is envious, lack of envy is the means of escape; for a person who is stingy, lack of stinginess is the means of escape;
for a person who is deceitful, lack of deceit is the means of escape.
For a person who is deceitful, freedom from deceit is the means of escape;
for a person who is stubborn, lack of stubbornness is the means of escape; for a person who is arrogant, lack of arrogance is the means of escape;
for a person who is difficult to speak with, being easy to speak with is the means of escape; for a person who has evil friends...
Having virtuous friends is a means of recovery; for a heedless person, heedfulness is a means of recovery;
for a person lacking faith, faith is a means of recovery; for a person lacking a sense of shame, a sense of shame is a means of recovery;
for a person lacking a sense of dread, a sense of dread is a means of recovery.
For a person who has heard little, great learning is the means of overcoming that state;
for a person who is lazy, the arousal of energy is the means of overcoming that state; for a person who is muddled in mindfulness, established mindfulness is the means of overcoming that state;
for a person who lacks wisdom, the perfection of wisdom is the means of overcoming that state.

For a person who clings to their own views, who is obstinate and tenacious, and who is difficult to release from them, the state of not clinging to views, being non-obstinate and non-tenacious, and being easy to release from them, serves as a means of escape.
4. The Discourse on the Upper Portion:
Just as, Cunda, whatever unwholesome states there may be, they all lead downward; and whatever wholesome states there may be, they all lead upward.
In the same way, Cunda, for a person who is harmful, non-harming becomes his higher part; for a person who takes life, abstaining from taking life becomes his higher part...

[and so on] ...for a person who clings to his own views, holds them fast, and is difficult to disabuse of them, not clinging to views, not holding them fast, and being easy to disabuse of them becomes his higher part.
5. The Discourse on Final Nibbāna.
"Cunda, it is impossible that one who is himself mired in the mud should pull out another who is mired in the mud.
But, Cunda, it is possible that one who is himself not mired in the mud should pull out another who is mired in the mud.
It is impossible, Cunda, that one who is himself untamed, undisciplined, and not fully extinguished should tame another, discipline another, or lead another to full extinction."
“Indeed, Cunda, it is possible that one who has tamed, trained, and attained final Nibbāna by himself will tame, train, and lead others to final Nibbāna.

In the same way, Cunda, for a person who is harmful, non-harming becomes the means for his final Nibbāna; for a person who takes life, abstaining from taking life becomes the means for his final Nibbāna;
for a person who takes what is not given, abstaining from taking what is not given becomes the means for his final Nibbāna.”
For a person who is unchaste, the abstention from unchastity leads to final Nibbāna.
For a person who speaks falsehood, the abstention from false speech leads to final Nibbāna.
For a person who speaks maliciously, the abstention from malicious speech leads to final Nibbāna.
For a person of harsh speech, abstaining from harsh speech leads to final Nibbāna.
For a person of idle chatter, abstaining from idle chatter leads to final Nibbāna.
For a person of covetousness, non-covetousness leads to final Nibbāna.
For a person with a mind of ill will, non-ill will arises for the sake of final Nibbāna.
For a person with wrong view, right view arises for the sake of final Nibbāna.
For a person with wrong intention, right intention arises for the sake of final Nibbāna.
For a person of wrong speech, right speech leads to final Nibbāna.
For a person of wrong action, right action leads to final Nibbāna.
For a person of wrong livelihood, right livelihood leads to final Nibbāna.
For a person of wrong effort, right effort arises for the sake of final Nibbāna.
For a person of wrong mindfulness, right mindfulness arises for the sake of final Nibbāna.
For a person of wrong concentration, right concentration arises for the sake of final Nibbāna.
For a person of wrong knowledge, right knowledge arises for the sake of final Nibbāna.
For a person of wrong liberation, right liberation arises for the sake of final Nibbāna.
For a person overwhelmed by sloth and torpor, the state of being free from sloth and torpor arises for the sake of final Nibbāna.
For an agitated person, non-agitation exists for the sake of final nibbāna.
For a person full of doubt, the crossing beyond doubt exists for the sake of final nibbāna.
For an angry person, non-anger exists for the sake of final nibbāna.
For a person who is resentful, non-resentment leads to final Nibbāna.
For a person who is contemptuous, non-contempt leads to final Nibbāna.
For a person who is spiteful, non-spite leads to final Nibbāna.
For a person who is envious, non-envy is the state of final Nirvana.
For a person who is miserly, non-miserliness is the state of final Nirvana.
For a person who is deceitful, non-deceitfulness is the state of final Nirvana.
For a person who is deceitful, non-deceitfulness leads to final Nibbāna.
For a person who is stubborn, non-stubbornness leads to final Nibbāna.
For a person who is arrogant, non-arrogance leads to final Nibbāna.
For a person who is difficult to speak with, being easy to speak with leads to final Nibbāna.
For a person who has evil friends, having virtuous friends leads to final Nibbāna.
For a person who is negligent, heedfulness leads to final Nibbāna.
In a person who lacks faith, faith arises for the sake of final Nibbāna.
In a person who lacks moral shame, moral shame arises for the sake of final Nibbāna.
In a person who lacks moral dread, moral dread arises for the sake of final Nibbāna.
For a person of little learning, great erudition leads to final Nibbāna.
For a person who is indolent, the arousal of energy leads to final Nibbāna.
For a person of muddled mindfulness, established mindfulness leads to final Nibbāna.
For a person of poor wisdom, the perfection of wisdom leads to final Nibbāna.

For a person who clings to their own views, who holds them supreme, who is stubborn, and who finds it hard to relinquish them, the state of not clinging to one's own views, not holding them supreme, not being stubborn, and easily relinquishing them leads to final Nibbāna.

Thus, Cunda, I have taught the method of effacement; I have taught the method of the arising of the mind; I have taught the method of circumambulation; I have taught the method of the higher part; and I have taught the method of final Nibbāna.
“Cunda, whatever was to be done by a Teacher out of compassion, seeking the welfare of his disciples, has been done for you by me.
Here, Cunda, are the roots of trees; here are empty huts. Meditate, Cunda, do not be negligent, and do not later fall into regret. This, Cunda, is our instruction.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The Venerable Mahācunda, gladdened, rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
Forty-four phrases were spoken,
and five underlying intentions were taught.
The discourse named "Effacement" is profound, like the ocean.
The eighth discourse, the Sallekha Sutta, is finished.
